prompt: What does eventual consistency guarantee?
hint: Read the definition for what it leaves out.

choices.text: Every read sees the latest write within one second
choices.why: No time bound is promised at all.

choices.text: If writes stop, every copy ends with the same value
choices.why: Right, and nothing about how long or what is seen meanwhile.

choices.text: Copies never disagree once a write has returned
choices.why: That is strong consistency.

choices.text: Writes are applied in the same order on every copy, everywhere
choices.why: Order is one of the things it leaves open.

prompt: Which of these is NOT left open by the definition of eventual consistency?
hint: One item is the definition itself.

choices.text: How long the copies take to agree
choices.why: Left open: "eventually" has no bound.

choices.text: What a reader sees in the meantime
choices.why: Left open; that is what session guarantees address.

choices.text: That idle copies converge to one value
choices.why: Right: convergence is the one thing it promises.

choices.text: Which concurrent write survives
choices.why: Left open; the lesson's last-writer-wins section is about it.

prompt: Which of these is a copy that can be stale, even though nobody designed it as a copy?
hint: Something sits in front of a service and answers for it.

choices.text: A primary database that every write goes to
choices.why: The primary is the owner, not a copy.

choices.text: A cache in front of the catalogue service
choices.why: Right: it answers from what it stored earlier.

choices.text: A synchronous standby that is never read from
choices.why: It is never read, so nobody sees it stale.

choices.text: The stock service in the lab, with its versions
choices.why: The stock service is the owner of the numbers.

prompt: Match each term to what it means.
hint: One of them is about one person, not about everybody.

pairs.right: once a write returns, every read anywhere sees it
copies agree once the writes stop
a person's reads see that person's own writes
a person never sees a version older than one already seen

prompt: In the lab, where does the shop get the number it shows on a product page?
hint: Look at `do_GET` in `shop.py`.

choices.text: It calls the stock service on every request
choices.why: Only when `?after=` says its copy is behind.

choices.text: It reads the stock service's database directly
choices.why: The stock service keeps its numbers in memory, and no module reads another's data.

choices.text: From its own copy, fed by events
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: From the other shop, which it asks first
choices.why: The shops share events, not reads.

prompt: Right after `PUT /stock/coffee` with 12, both shops answered "no copy yet". What does that show?
hint: Three seconds later shop b had it.

choices.text: The event was lost and had to be resent
choices.why: It arrived without being resent.

choices.text: The shops were misconfigured
choices.why: Nothing was misconfigured.

choices.text: The event was still on its way to them
choices.why: Right: the window, on a system that works.

choices.text: The broker refused the event
choices.why: Then the stock service would have answered 503.

prompt: Why does `stock.py` publish the event before keeping the change?
hint: Think about a broker that is down.

choices.text: To make the shops' copies update a little faster
choices.why: The order does not change the copies' speed.

choices.text: So a failed publish changes nothing and returns 503
choices.why: Right: the owner never holds a change the copies will never hear about.

choices.text: Because pika needs the exchange to exist first
choices.why: pika has no opinion about it.

choices.text: To give the event a version
choices.why: The version is computed before either step.

prompt: On an idle system, how long was shop b's window in the lab?
hint: Count the half-second reads that still said 12.

choices.text: About twenty seconds
choices.why: That was after the burst of ten changes.

choices.text: About two seconds, its LAG
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Zero; it updated at once
choices.why: Four reads in a row still said 12.

choices.text: About a fifth of a second
choices.why: That is shop a's time per event.

prompt: A copy handles one event in 0.5 seconds and has 40 events waiting in its queue. Roughly how many seconds old is what it shows for the last change?
hint: Queue length times time per event.

prompt: Why does the window tend to be longest when the most customers are looking?
hint: What does a busy afternoon do to the queue?

choices.text: Because the broker slows down under load by design
choices.why: The broker was not the slow part.

choices.text: Because customers' reads block the consumer
choices.why: Reads and the consumer did not compete in the lab.

choices.text: Busier times mean more changes queued for the copy
choices.why: Right: window = queue length × time per event.

choices.text: Because the owner holds a lock while customers read
choices.why: The owner's lock is held only while publishing.

prompt: Which measure tells you, in time, how far behind a copy is?
hint: One of them counts messages, not seconds.

choices.text: The number of messages in its queue
choices.why: That is in messages; it says nothing about how old they are.

choices.text: The age of the newest event it has applied
choices.why: Right, given that each event carries when it was created.

choices.text: The number of requests it answers per second
choices.why: Busy and behind are different things.

choices.text: Whether its health check passes
choices.why: A copy that is behind is perfectly healthy.

prompt: Who is harmed most by the inconsistency window?
hint: Who knows what the number should be?

choices.text: A customer browsing the catalogue
choices.why: They cannot tell 12 from 11.

choices.text: The person who just made the change
choices.why: Right: they know the old value is wrong.

choices.text: The stock service, which owns the number
choices.why: The owner is never behind itself.

choices.text: The broker that carries the events
choices.why: The broker does not read stock.

prompt: What does `?after=13` make shop b do when its copy is at version 12?
hint: Look at the answer it gave in the lab.

choices.text: Wait until version 13 arrives
choices.why: It does not wait in this lab.

choices.text: Refuse the request with an error
choices.why: It answers.

choices.text: Answer from its copy and warn
choices.why: The copy is not used when it is behind.

choices.text: Ask the stock service and say so
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Why is read-your-writes much cheaper than strong consistency?
hint: To whom is the promise made?

choices.text: It is promised to one person, about their own changes
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It needs no version numbers
choices.why: The lab's version of it needs one.

choices.text: It works only while the copy is never behind the owner
choices.why: It exists for when the copy lags.

choices.text: It skips the broker
choices.why: The events still go through the broker.

prompt: "After a person writes, send their reads to the owner for the next minute." What is the weakness?
hint: How long is the window?

choices.text: It sends every customer's reads to the owner
choices.why: Only the reads of the person who wrote.

choices.text: The minute is a guess; a longer window breaks it
choices.why: Right: the window has no bound.

choices.text: The owner is unable to answer reads quickly enough
choices.why: The owner answers reads in the lab.

choices.text: It requires a version number in every single event
choices.why: That is the other approach.

prompt: In the lab, the customer saw 7 and then 0. Why?
hint: Which shop answered each request?

choices.text: The real stock went from 7 down to 0 in between
choices.why: The owner went from 0 to 7.

choices.text: The second read reached a copy further behind
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Shop b applied an old event twice
choices.why: Nothing was resent in that section.

choices.text: The load balancer cached the first answer
choices.why: There was no cache; two copies answered.

prompt: Which fix gives monotonic reads without tying a person to one copy?
hint: The same mechanism as read-your-writes.

choices.text: Sticky sessions
choices.why: That is the one that ties a person to one copy.

choices.text: Making every copy handle events at the same speed
choices.why: Copies are never exactly in step.

choices.text: Sending the highest version seen along with every read
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Removing the slower copy
choices.why: Some copy is always the slower one.

prompt: What is the weakness of sticky sessions for monotonic reads?
hint: What happens to the copy a person is stuck to?

choices.text: They need a version in every event
choices.why: They need no version at all.

choices.text: That copy restarts, and load spreads unevenly
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They send every read to the owner instead of a copy
choices.why: Reads stay on the copy.

choices.text: They are only offered by some brokers
choices.why: A load balancer offers them, not a broker.

prompt: After version 15 was sent again, shop b said 5 and the owner said 4. When would shop b have corrected itself?
hint: What would bring a new event?

choices.text: After its LAG of two seconds
choices.why: The LAG had passed; it had applied the old event.

choices.text: When the broker noticed the duplicate
choices.why: The broker does not compare contents.

choices.text: When coffee next changed
choices.why: Right: the copy converged on a wrong value.

choices.text: Never; restarting it would keep 5
choices.why: A restart empties the in-memory copy.

prompt: What does `CHECK_VERSION=1` make the shop do?
hint: Read the shop's log after the second resend.

choices.text: Ignore an event no newer than the version it holds
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Ask the owner before applying each event
choices.why: It never asks the owner while applying.

choices.text: Apply events in the order of their timestamps
choices.why: The events carry versions, not timestamps.

choices.text: Reject the resent event at the broker, before delivery
choices.why: The broker delivers it; the shop decides.

prompt: Why must the version come from the owner rather than from each machine's clock?
hint: Two clocks can disagree.

choices.text: Clocks are too coarse to tell two close events apart
choices.why: Resolution is not the main problem.

choices.text: Only the owner orders the changes to that thing
choices.why: Right: clocks drift, and the later change can carry the earlier time.

choices.text: Versions are smaller than timestamps
choices.why: Size is not the point.

choices.text: The broker rejects messages that carry a timestamp
choices.why: It does not.

prompt: Which event can be applied in any order, any number of times, and still converge?
hint: State, or a change?

choices.text: "Two bags of coffee sold"
choices.why: Applied twice, it sells four.

choices.text: "Coffee went down by one"
choices.why: Still a change; repeats and order matter.

choices.text: "Coffee is 4, version 18"
choices.why: Right, with a copy that keeps the newest version.

choices.text: "Restock coffee"
choices.why: A command, not a state.

prompt: With `MERGE=lww`, what happened to Ana's tea?
hint: Look at both baskets five seconds later.

choices.text: It stayed in shop a only
choices.why: Both copies ended the same.

choices.text: An error said it conflicted
choices.why: There was no error at all.

choices.text: It disappeared from both copies without an error
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It replaced the coffee in both
choices.why: The later basket, with coffee, won.

prompt: For which data is last writer wins a reasonable rule?
hint: When does the newer write really replace the older?

choices.text: A shopping basket edited on two devices
choices.why: Both edits were meant; one is lost.

choices.text: A customer's delivery address
choices.why: Right: the newer one is the one they want.

choices.text: A count of units sold
choices.why: Each sale counts; dropping one loses money.

choices.text: Comments posted on a product
choices.why: Each comment is its own; none replaces another.

prompt: With `MERGE=union`, why did the tea come back after being removed?
hint: What did shop b still have when it published?

choices.text: Shop a's DELETE failed and left the tea in place
choices.why: It answered with coffee only.

choices.text: The broker redelivered an older basket to shop a
choices.why: It was shop b's new publish.

choices.text: The version check rejected the removal as too old
choices.why: Baskets carry no version.

choices.text: Union cannot tell a removal from a missing item
choices.why: Right.

prompt: For most systems, what is the simplest way to avoid reconciling concurrent writes?
hint: The last row of the table.

choices.text: Use a CRDT for every type of data in the system
choices.why: Correct for some data, and far from the simplest.

choices.text: Give each thing one owner; copies only read
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Synchronise every server's clock with NTP first
choices.why: Clocks still drift, and both writes were meant.

choices.text: Keep both versions and ask the user to choose
choices.why: That is reconciling, not avoiding it.

prompt: Match each way of handling concurrent writes to what it does.
hint: Which one loses a write, and which one can bring one back?

pairs.right: keeps the newest stamp, drops the rest
keeps all items; removals can return
hands every concurrent version to the reader
a type whose merge is always right for its kind

prompt: After the checkout creates an order, what should the next page show?
hint: The cheapest read-your-writes.

choices.text: The order list, read from a copy
choices.why: The copy may not have the order yet.

choices.text: The write's own answer
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A spinner until every copy has it
choices.why: Copies have no bound; the spinner might never stop.

choices.text: Nothing, to avoid showing stale data
choices.why: A person who sees nothing assumes it failed.

prompt: A product page shows the coffee count from a copy. What should it say?
hint: The exact count belongs at checkout.

choices.text: The exact count, refreshed every second
choices.why: Still a copy, still possibly behind.

choices.text: Nothing about stock at all
choices.why: The approximate number is still useful.

choices.text: An approximate "only a few left"
choices.why: Right; the owner decides at checkout.

choices.text: The number from the other copy too
choices.why: Two copies on one screen is the disagreement made visible.

prompt: Which decision must be made at the owner and not from a copy?
hint: Which mistake costs money?

choices.text: Showing a product's photo
choices.why: Yesterday's photo is harmless.

choices.text: Listing products in a category
choices.why: A list a moment old is fine.

choices.text: Showing a basket's item count in the header
choices.why: It should match the basket page, but a moment's lag costs nothing.

choices.text: Taking the last bag of coffee when the customer pays
choices.why: Right.

hint: Change, change, wait, resend, look.

prompt: Quitanda's search page is fed from the catalogue by events, and a member of staff complains that a price they changed "does not save". What is the most likely cause and fix?
hint: Did the change fail, or is the reader looking at a copy?

choices.text: The catalogue is losing writes; make its replication synchronous
choices.why: The owner had the change.

choices.text: The page reads a copy that is behind; show staff the owner's answer
choices.why: Right: read-your-writes.

choices.text: The broker is dropping events; move the events to Kafka instead
choices.why: Nothing points at the broker.

choices.text: The price has two owners; resolve it with last writer wins
choices.why: There is one owner: the catalogue.
